title: Algebraic Data Type
body:
How you define your own types in [[Haskell]]. A type is built from two combinators, and the
name is literal: the number of values a type has is the sum or the product of its parts'.

```haskell
data Colour = Red | Green | Blue                   -- sum:     3 values
data Point  = Point Double Double                  -- product: |Double| x |Double|
data Shape  = Circle Double | Rect Double Double   -- both
```

| | Reads as | Values | In [[C]] | In [[Java]] |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sum** (`\|`) | "one of these" | $\|A\| + \|B\|$ | `enum`, or a tagged `union` you check by hand | a sealed hierarchy, or an `instanceof` chain |
| **Product** | "all of these" | $\|A\| \times \|B\|$ | `struct` | a class with fields |

The product half is nothing new; it is a [[Structure|struct]] with a constructor name. The sum half is the
one C and Java handle badly, and it is the reason the feature matters. A C `union` does not
record which member is live, so you keep a tag alongside it and nothing checks that you read
the member the tag says. Here the tag *is* the type.

## Pattern matching is the eliminator

Constructors build values; pattern matching is the only way to take them apart, and it is the
other half of the feature rather than a convenience:

```haskell
area :: Shape -> Double
area (Circle r)   = pi * r * r
area (Rect w h)   = w * h
```

The compiler knows every constructor, so it can tell you when a match is **non-exhaustive**.
Add `Triangle` to `Shape` and every incomplete `case` in the program becomes a warning with a
file and a line. That is the concrete payoff of [[Static Typing]] here: the type system turns
"I added a variant" into a work list instead of a run-time surprise.

Patterns nest and bind at once, which is why [[Recursion Schemes]] reads the way it does:
`f (x : xs) = ...` matches the list constructor and names both parts in one line.

## `Maybe` and the null problem

The single most-cited example, and worth understanding as a design argument rather than a
library type:

```haskell
data Maybe a = Nothing | Just a

safeDiv :: Int -> Int -> Maybe Int
safeDiv _ 0 = Nothing
safeDiv x y = Just (x `div` y)
```

In [[Java]] any reference may be `null` and nothing in the type says whether this one might be,
so the check is a discipline you either remember or do not. Here `Maybe Int` and `Int` are
different types: you cannot use a `Maybe Int` as a number without matching on it first, and a
plain `Int` can never be missing. **The possibility of absence is in the type, and it is
absent from every type that did not ask for it.** `Either e a` is the same move for errors,
carrying a reason rather than just a failure.

That is also where [[Monad]] enters: chaining several `Maybe`-returning calls by hand is a
staircase of nested cases, and `>>=` is exactly the operation that flattens it.

## Recursive types

A type may mention itself, which is how the data structures from [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] are
written here:

```haskell
data List a = Nil | Cons a (List a)
data Tree a = Leaf | Node (Tree a) a (Tree a)
```

Every such definition has base constructors and recursive ones, so a function over it has base
cases and recursive cases in exactly the same shape. That correspondence is not a coincidence
and it is the whole of [[Program Correctness]]: structural induction over `Tree` has one case
per constructor, and so does any function that consumes one.

## Core Facts to Know

- Two combinators: **sum** (`|`, one of) and **product** (fields, all of).
- The names are literal: value counts add for sums, multiply for products.
- A sum type is a `union` that cannot be read as the wrong member.
- Constructors build; **pattern matching** is the only way to take apart.
- The compiler warns on non-exhaustive matches, so adding a constructor gives you a work list.
- `Maybe a = Nothing | Just a` puts the possibility of absence into the type.
- A plain `Int` therefore cannot be null; no discipline required.
- `Either e a` is the same idea carrying an error value.
- Recursive types have base and recursive constructors, mirroring base and recursive cases.
- That mirroring is what makes structural induction apply. See [[Program Correctness]].
